blocks.text: Are the loopholes finally closed?

inlines.text: Are the loopholes finally closed?

blocks.text: Jordan Schneider and Lily Ottinger

inlines.text: Jordan Schneider
and
Lily Ottinger

blocks.text: A 132-page export control rule landed Monday morning, and the Commerce Department’s own press release credited Treasury and the NSC with writing it. Days after the Megaspeed scandal ended Jensen Huang’s run at Nvidia, Washington is moving to close the cloud loophole that, by ChinaTalk’s estimate, supplies two-fifths of China’s AI compute.

inlines.text: A 132-page export control rule landed Monday morning, and the Commerce Department’s own press release credited Treasury and the NSC with writing it. Days after the Megaspeed scandal ended Jensen Huang’s run at Nvidia, Washington is moving to close the cloud loophole that, by ChinaTalk’s estimate, supplies two-fifths of China’s AI compute.

blocks.text: Two Biden NSC alumni weigh in: ⁠Chris McGuire⁠, now senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations after a stint as deputy senior director for technology and national security, and ⁠Julian Gewirtz⁠, the former senior director for China and Taiwan affairs now a senior research scholar at Columbia SIPA.

inlines.text: Two Biden NSC alumni weigh in:
⁠Chris McGuire⁠
, now senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations after a stint as deputy senior director for technology and national security, and
⁠Julian Gewirtz⁠
, the former senior director for China and Taiwan affairs now a senior research scholar at Columbia SIPA.

blocks.text: We discuss…

inlines.text: We discuss…
Three loopholes closed in 132 pages
— license requirements for chips headed to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil; a cap on compute rented to Chinese firms; and a TSMC backdoor closed for the second time.
The Northern Virginia problem
— why a rule that stops at the US border could simply move China’s rented compute from Johor to the Washington suburbs.
Who wrote the rule
— what crediting Treasury and the NSC says about Commerce’s credibility, and whether Trump holds firm in Shenzhen.
Does Xi know the numbers
— whether Beijing escalates or doubles down on the bet that it can (again) talk Trump into loosening controls.
Jensen’s soup vendor
— the customer-concentration fear that pushed Nvidia toward Asian neoclouds and China.
Zero consequences for three million chips
— why export controls need their BNP Paribas moment, and what that has to do with AI safety.

blocks.text: The rule addresses three categories:

inlines.text: The rule addresses three categories:
Countering Chinese smuggling of AI chips.
Restricting Chinese companies from renting access to AI chips.
Closing loopholes that let Chinese companies make AI chips at TSMC, Samsung, and elsewhere.

blocks.text: Those are the three ways it tries to cut down China’s access to compute. My top line, as I said at the start, is that this is a good rule that actually moves the ball forward. It closes multiple real loopholes. It is also imperfect. When you close some loopholes, others become more important, so we need to take a few additional actions to tighten things up. But this is real forward progress.

inlines.text: Let me break down those three buckets.

blocks.text: Smuggling

inlines.text: Smuggling

blocks.text: Chris McGuire: This one is straightforward. The rule imposes controls on Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil. Southeast Asia in particular has become a massive smuggling hub for AI chips over the last few years. Relative to the size of their economies, Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, and Indonesia were the third-, fourth-, fifth-, and eighth-largest importers of AI chips in the world — way, way more than anyone else relative to GDP. They basically displaced China: all the demand that was previously going to China went to these countries. Brazil is also setting up large AI data centers for ByteDance and others, which is presumably why it was added.

blocks.text: This is positive, but it will push smuggling to other countries. Without something broader, smugglers will inevitably move from Malaysia to Bhutan or Nepal or somewhere else. Still, the countries that are currently the biggest hubs now have to get a license from the US government before their companies can buy the chips.

blocks.text: What we need to move toward is a general policy: if you’re buying hundreds of millions of dollars of AI chips anywhere in the world, the US government should at least have visibility into that, if not the ability to veto it. That can and should be done in a follow-up rule.

blocks.text: Remote access

inlines.text: Remote access

blocks.text: Chris McGuire: Restricting Chinese companies from renting access to AI chips is a notable new development. On smuggling, the Trump administration simply hadn’t been enforcing the anti-smuggling regulations the Biden administration put into effect. But on remote access, regulations like this didn’t exist at all. So this is new, and it’s positive.

inlines.text: Chris McGuire:

Restricting Chinese companies from renting access to AI chips is a notable new development. On smuggling, the Trump administration simply hadn’t been enforcing the anti-smuggling regulations the Biden administration put into effect. But on remote access, regulations like this didn’t exist at all. So this is new, and it’s positive.

blocks.text: The rule says that if you hold large numbers of AI chips, you can rent only a fairly small number to Chinese companies without applying for a license from Commerce — the equivalent of roughly 200 of the most advanced Blackwell chips, or about 800 H100s. That’s a meaningful number of chips, but training or running frontier models takes thousands, tens of thousands, maybe hundreds of thousands of chips. So this would significantly curtail China’s access.

inlines.text: The rule says that if you hold large numbers of AI chips, you can rent only a fairly small number to Chinese companies without applying for a license from Commerce — the equivalent of roughly 200 of the most advanced Blackwell chips, or about 800 H100s. blocks.text: It also applies retroactively. The rule effectively says this has always been the policy: if you were providing at least half of your computing power to Chinese companies, that was itself a violation of the controls. If that’s actually enforced, it means they could go after Megaspeed and say it was violating controls by providing compute to China. We’ll see how enforcement goes, but it’s a very strong signal that they don’t want this to happen.

blocks.text: There’s one huge loophole, though: the rule doesn’t apply inside the United States. Until that’s closed, Chinese companies will divert all their computing power away from Johor, Malaysia, and into Northern Virginia. Northern Virginia is going to become the center of China AI until we fix this. Commerce has the authority to close this right now, and it needs to get done.

blocks.text: Chip design at TSMC

inlines.text: Chip design at TSMC

blocks.text: Chris McGuire: The last piece blocks Chinese chip designers from making AI chips at TSMC, which is good and important. The Biden administration put regulations in place requiring any company making an AI chip at TSMC to apply for a license unless it was on a whitelist. Not many companies make these chips, so all the legitimate ones were already on the whitelist. For various arcane regulatory reasons, that rule hadn’t been in effect, and Commerce hadn’t been enforcing it. Now it’s back in effect, and they say they’ll enforce it.

inlines.text: Chris McGuire:

The last piece blocks Chinese chip designers from making AI chips at TSMC, which is good and important. The Biden administration put regulations in place requiring any company making an AI chip at TSMC to apply for a license unless it was on a whitelist. Not many companies make these chips, so all the legitimate ones were already on the whitelist. For various arcane regulatory reasons, that rule hadn’t been in effect, and Commerce hadn’t been enforcing it. Now it’s back in effect, and they say they’ll enforce it.

blocks.text: They actually went a step further: any Chinese company making a chip at 14 nanometers or more advanced has to apply for a license, regardless of whether it claims the chip is for AI (there are some technical parameters on that). That means, for example, Xiaomi has to apply for a license to make a three-nanometer smartphone chip at TSMC. So the implications go beyond AI. This is great for Qualcomm and other US companies that would like to sell smartphone chips to China, since China has been designing its own chips at TSMC and US firms may now capture more of that market. But the purpose isn’t to give them an advantage. The purpose is to cut off every avenue for Chinese circumvention, because we know China has illicitly made millions of chips at TSMC.

That loophole needs to be closed tomorrow. But these are signs of life, and a recognition that export controls are something we’re going to do, and that US advantages in computing power actually matter.

blocks.text: Julian Gewirtz: It’s striking to see that language in the Commerce press release — not because this is the first time in history the NSC has helped draft a Commerce regulation (I’ll refrain from comment, given I’m here with my former NSC colleague), but because it signals one thing above all: the administration knows Commerce is low on credibility, in Washington and more generally. We may read it as palace intrigue about the drafting, but to me it’s also about the credibility of the signal. It’s an attempt to say this regulation can stand up and should be expected to last.

blocks.text: My concern is that when President Trump spoke about these dynamics this morning, he took it right back to the palace intrigue — to Lutnick and Bessent disagreeing on how to approach China policy — and seemed pretty unaware that his administration had just rolled out a major new regulation. That matters because the president is heading to China, where he’s about to sit across the table from people who do not want these regulations on the books. There’s a version of events where we hold fast to this, and there’s a version where he gets wobbly pretty quickly.

We’ll see the same rampant smuggling, undeterred. We need a change in attitude and perspective at Commerce for this to be effective at all, and I’m not convinced the current leadership can make that happen.

blocks.text: You saw the comments Dylan and others made about wanting to preserve the ability to cut the Chinese off from cloud access. But that’s not where we are. It’s not as if Chinese firms have been accessing compute through AWS or Microsoft, with all the money flowing to American companies and the US holding the lever. blocks.text: But I can’t get out of my head that there’s a strong ideological dimension too — a vision of what an “international technology ecosystem” ought to look like, one in which the world-leading US companies are needed by everybody. For years, I’ve felt that vision is out of step with where Beijing sees the future going. Beijing’s ideal version of this transitional period is one in which it publicly asserts that it’s pursuing self-reliance and making breakthrough after breakthrough on an indigenous tech stack, while in fact getting the benefit of world-leading American technology through third-country remote access, smuggling, and all the other channels Chris has described. That two-track model isn’t designed to last. It’s designed to be something Beijing outgrows as quickly as possible — but they’re not there yet.

blocks.text: That’s a very telling story. It explains why Nvidia wanted to sell to all these neoclouds in Asia, and potentially even to China. They’re worried about the concentration of their customer base among a very small number of US hyperscalers and providers. There aren’t many companies that can buy $100 or $200 billion of AI chips a year. Nvidia’s revenues are crazy high, and it makes extremely expensive products that everyone wants, but there are only so many companies it can sell to. If any of them decided to go with AMD, or to make its own chips, Nvidia could face a huge revenue drop-off right away. So it wants a more diverse customer base.
